Early Apologists
UR-lee uh-POL-oh-jists
noun phrase (second-century defenders of the faith)
From “apologist” (Greek apologia, a reasoned defence); the second- and early-third-century Christian writers—Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian, and others—who defended the faith against pagan slander and heresy.

📖 Biblical Definition

The early apologists were the Christian writers of the second and early third centuries who defended the faith against the slanders of paganism and the corruptions of heresy. Among the chief were Justin Martyr, who reasoned with the philosophers and sealed his witness with his blood; Irenaeus of Lyons, who refuted the Gnostics in Against Heresies and insisted on the apostolic deposit and the rule of faith; Tertullian of Carthage, the fierce Latin advocate who coined much of the church's Trinitarian vocabulary; and others such as Athenagoras and Theophilus. They answered the false charges of atheism, cannibalism, and disloyalty hurled against the Christians, set forth the reasonableness of the faith before emperors and magistrates, and contended for the truth against the Gnostic denial of the Creator, the goodness of the flesh, and the true humanity of Christ. The dictionary honours the early apologists as obeying the apostolic charge to be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh a reason of the hope within them, and as earnestly contending for the faith once delivered unto the saints. They stand as a model of bold, reasoned witness in a hostile world, and Irenaeus especially as an early and valuable guard of the apostolic gospel against heresy. Yet the dictionary weighs them by the Word and not the reverse. Some of the apologists, reasoning with Greek philosophy, leaned too far toward it—Justin's notion of the logos spermatikos conceded too much to the philosophers, and seeds of the later sacramentalism and works-righteousness can be traced among them. They were honourable fathers, not infallible authorities; the dictionary receives their defence of the faith with gratitude while trying every word of theirs by Scripture, the sole and final rule.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The second- and early-third-century defenders of the faith—Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian, and others—who answered pagan slander and refuted heresy; honoured as bold, reasoned witnesses, yet weighed by the Word and not made infallible.

EARLY APOLOGISTS, noun phrase. [Greek apologia, a defence.] The second-century Christian defenders of the faith.

Justin Martyr reasoned with the philosophers and died for Christ.

Irenaeus refuted the Gnostics in Against Heresies.

Tertullian of Carthage shaped the church's Trinitarian vocabulary.

Honoured as bold witnesses, yet tried by Scripture and not made infallible.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Pe 3:15 — "But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:"

Jude 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

Php 1:7 — "Even as it is meet for me to think this of you all, because I have you in my heart; inasmuch as both in my bonds, and in the defence and confirmation of the gospel, ye all are partakers of my grace."

Ac 17:17 — "Therefore disputed he in the synagogue with the Jews, and with the devout persons, and in the market daily with them that met with him."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Some early apologists, reasoning with Greek philosophy, conceded too much to it, and seeds of later sacramentalism appear among them; they were honourable fathers, not infallible authorities, and must be tried by the Word.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours the early apologists for genuine and great labour: they answered the slanders of atheism, cannibalism, and disloyalty hurled at the church, set the reasonableness of the faith before hostile emperors, and contended against the Gnostic heresies that denied the Creator, the goodness of the body, and the true humanity of Christ. Justin reasoned with the philosophers and sealed his witness with martyrdom; Irenaeus guarded the apostolic gospel and the rule of faith; Tertullian forged much of the church's Trinitarian language. They obeyed the charge to be ready always to give an answer, and earnestly contended for the faith once delivered. This is honourable history, received with gratitude.

Yet they must be weighed by the Word, not set above or beside it. Reasoning with Greek thought, some leaned too far toward it: Justin's logos spermatikos, finding seeds of the Word scattered among the pagan philosophers, conceded more to philosophy than Scripture warrants, and the seeds of later sacramentalism and a creeping works-righteousness can be traced among the fathers of this age. The dictionary applies its rule for figures outside the Reformed tradition: receive their defence of the faith and their refutation of heresy with thanks, honour their courage and their orthodoxy on the great matters, but try every word of theirs by Scripture, the sole and final rule. They were faithful fathers, not infallible authorities, and the canon closed at the apostles, not at their successors.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Greek apologia (a reasoned defence, as in a court); the second-century writers who gave a defence of the Christian faith before pagans and heretics.

expand to see more

Apologia, Greek, a reasoned defence or answer (1 Peter 3:15).

Justin Martyr, the philosopher-convert who died for Christ.

Irenaeus of Lyons, refuter of the Gnostics in Against Heresies.

Tertullian of Carthage, the fierce Latin defender of the faith.

Athenagoras, Theophilus, and others among their number.

Usage

"The teacher honoured the early apologists for answering pagan slander and refuting the Gnostics."

"He noted Irenaeus as an early guard of the apostolic gospel against heresy."

"She tried even Justin's words by Scripture, the sole and final rule of faith."
